summary: Describes the Russian federal standard for digital signatures, GOST R 34.10-2001, for generating and verifying signatures. It is informational and not a standard of the IETF.

eli5.summary: It explains a way to sign a message so others can tell it is yours and unchanged, as used in a Russian standard.

subtitle: The Russian federal digital signature standard, built on elliptic curves over a prime field.

tldr.problem: Russian cryptography was being used in Internet applications, and developers needed a written description of how GOST R 34.10-2001 signatures are generated and verified.
tldr.mechanism: A message is hashed, then a signature is computed from the hash, a private integer d and a fresh random integer k using multiples of a point P on an elliptic curve. The result is a 512-bit value made of two 256-bit halves, r and s.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5832 is Informational and not an IETF standard, and RFC 7091 later updated it. The RFC says the standard replaced GOST R 34.10-94 and that its resistance is estimated at 2^128 operations.

today: RFC 5832 is Informational and was updated by RFC 7091; it has not been obsoleted. The text states the algorithm replaces GOST R 34.10-94 and is obligatory in the Russian Federation for systems providing public services.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
GOST R 34.10-2001 describes how to generate and verify digital signatures using operations on the group of points of an elliptic curve defined over a prime finite field. It replaces GOST R 34.10-94, to increase security against unauthorized modification. The RFC states that it is obligatory to use in the Russian Federation in all data processing systems providing public services.

A signature gives three things for a transmitted message: integrity control, proof of the signatory's authorship and protection against forgery. Its security rests on the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem in the elliptic curve group and on the security of the hash function used, which is defined in GOST R 34.11-94 (see RFC 5831).

The scheme does not define how key pairs or parameter sets are generated. The RFC gives RFC 4357 as a source of possible parameter sets.
sections.eli5: The signature proves a message came from you and was not changed. It is safe because the math needed to forge it is extremely hard.

sections.title: Curve, Parameters and Keys
sections.content:
The curve is the set of points (x,y) satisfying y^2 = x^3 + a*x + b (mod p), with p a prime. Points can be added, and a point can be multiplied by an integer. The scheme parameters are:

  • p, the modulus, with p > 2^255.
  • The curve coefficients a and b, and the group order m.
  • q, a prime order of a cyclic subgroup, with 2^254 < q < 2^256.
  • A base point P with q*P = O.
  • A hash function mapping messages onto 256-bit vectors, defined in GOST R 34.11-94.

Each user has a signature key, an integer d with 0 < d < q, and a verification key, the point Q where d*P = Q. The parameters must also satisfy conditions such as p^t /= 1 (mod q) for all t from 1 up to some B with B >= 31, and m /= p.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on a shared curve and a starting point. Your private number is a secret count of hops from the starting point, and your public key is where you land.

sections.title: Generating a Signature
sections.content:
To sign a message M, Algorithm I runs these steps:

  • Hash the message: H = h(M).
  • Turn H into an integer and set e = alpha (mod q). If e = 0, use e = 1.
  • Generate a random (or pseudorandom) integer k with 0 < k < q.
  • Compute the point C = k*P and take r = x_C (mod q). If r = 0, go back and pick a new k.
  • Compute s = (r*d + k*e) (mod q). If s = 0, pick a new k again.
  • Convert r and s to 256-bit vectors R and S; the signature is R || S.

The signature is therefore a 512-bit binary vector, and it may be accompanied by a text field such as signer identifiers or a time label.
sections.eli5: You make a fingerprint of the message, pick a random secret number, and mix the fingerprint, the random number and your private number into two big numbers. Those two numbers are the signature.

sections.title: Verifying a Signature
sections.content:
To verify, Algorithm II takes the message, the signature and the verification key Q. It first splits the signature into r and s and checks that 0 < r < q and 0 < s < q; otherwise the signature is invalid.

It then hashes the message and computes e exactly as the signer did, and calculates v = e^(-1) (mod q), z1 = s*v (mod q) and z2 = -r*v (mod q). The point C = z1*P + z2*Q gives R = x_C (mod q). If R = r, the signature is accepted; otherwise it is invalid.
sections.eli5: The checker redoes part of the math using only your public key. If the answer lines up with the first signature number, the signature is real.

sections.title: Test Examples
sections.content:
Section 7 is a reference appendix of the original standard, not officially part of it. It lists one set of parameters p, a, b, m, q, P, a signature key d and a verification key Q in decimal and hexadecimal. These values are recommended only for testing the correctness of implementations.

It then shows the intermediate values for one run of signature generation (e, k, C, r and s) and for verification (v, z1, z2 and the recomputed point), where the recomputed R equals r. Appendix A adds extra terms from the digital signature area.
sections.eli5: The document includes one fully worked example with every number shown, so you can test your own program against it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The section opens by saying that this entire document is about security considerations. It estimates the current cryptographic resistance of the algorithm at 2^128 operations of multiple elliptic curve point computations on a prime modulus of order 2^256.

The RFC also says the scheme's security rests on the security of the hash function used.
sections.eli5: Forging a signature would take an astronomically large amount of work. The scheme also relies on a good fingerprint function.
